_meta.description: Knowledge base of REAL, currently-used spatial / single-cell analysis tools mapped to pipeline steps. Every entry is a real package with a real install command. 'maturity' and 'limitations' are honest. Nothing here is invented. Reviewed 2026-07; always confirm current version/API before running.
_meta.maturity_scale: mature (de-facto standard, stable) > established (widely used, actively maintained) > emerging (real & published, smaller user base) > research (published method, expect friction)
_meta.disclaimer: Runtimes are order-of-magnitude estimates on a typical workstation (8-16 cores, 32-64 GB RAM, one consumer GPU where noted). Real timing depends heavily on dataset size and hardware.

tools.name: Scanpy
tools.why: The backbone AnnData ecosystem. Nearly every other tool reads/writes its objects. Standard for QC, normalization, PCA, neighbors, Leiden clustering, and marker DE.
tools.code:
import scanpy as sc
adata = sc.read_h5ad('data.h5ad')
sc.pp.calculate_qc_metrics(adata, inplace=True, percent_top=None)
adata = adata[adata.obs.n_genes_by_counts > 200]
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)
sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(adata, n_top_genes=2000)
sc.pp.pca(adata); sc.pp.neighbors(adata); sc.tl.leiden(adata)
tools.runtime: Seconds to a few minutes for <500k cells; minutes for millions.
tools.limitations: QC thresholds are judgment calls, not defaults. Leiden resolution changes cluster count arbitrarily. Marker DE (rank_genes_groups) treats cells as independent replicates - do not use it for condition-level statistics.

tools.name: Squidpy
tools.why: Scanpy's spatial companion: spatial neighbor graphs, Moran's I spatial autocorrelation, neighborhood enrichment, ligand-receptor (ligrec), and platform readers (Visium/Xenium/Vizgen/nanostring).
tools.code:
import squidpy as sq
sq.gr.spatial_neighbors(adata, coord_type='generic', n_neighs=6)
sq.gr.spatial_autocorr(adata, mode='moran')  # spatially variable genes
sq.gr.nhood_enrichment(adata, cluster_key='leiden')
tools.runtime: Seconds to minutes; neighbor graph scales with cell count.
tools.limitations: Moran's I flags spatial structure but not biological cause. Ligrec is permutation-based and database-dependent; treat as hypothesis generation.

tools.name: SpatialData / spatialdata-io
tools.why: Unified reader/representation across Visium, Visium HD, Xenium, MERSCOPE, CosMx, Stereo-seq. Keeps images, transcripts, shapes, and tables in one coordinate system - the cleanest way to start a multi-platform pipeline.
tools.code:
import spatialdata_io
sdata = spatialdata_io.xenium('path/to/xenium_output/')
# sdata.tables['table'] is an AnnData; sdata.points, sdata.images, sdata.shapes
sdata.write('experiment.zarr')
tools.runtime: Seconds to minutes depending on image size; Zarr backing helps with large data.
tools.limitations: Younger API than scanpy; expect occasional breaking changes. Large images need on-disk (Zarr/Dask) handling to avoid OOM.

tools.name: Sopa
tools.why: Technology-agnostic pipeline that orchestrates segmentation (Cellpose/Baysor/others) and QC on top of SpatialData, with tiling for memory-safe processing of large imaging datasets. Good glue when you want a reproducible imaging pipeline rather than hand-wiring tools.
tools.code:
# CLI-driven; core idea:
# sopa segmentation cellpose  experiment.zarr --diameter 30 --channels DAPI
# sopa aggregate experiment.zarr --gene-column feature_name
import sopa
sdata = sopa.io.xenium('path/to/xenium/')
tools.runtime: Minutes to hours for large imaging datasets (segmentation-bound).
tools.limitations: Still maturing; it orchestrates other tools' failure modes rather than removing them. Segmentation quality is still whatever the chosen backend produces.

tools.name: Stereopy
tools.why: BGI's official toolkit for Stereo-seq: reads GEF/GEM, does binning (bin20/bin50), cell segmentation from the ssDNA image, and standard clustering at scale.
tools.code:
import stereo as st
data = st.io.read_gef('SN.gef', bin_size=50)
data.tl.cal_qc()
data.tl.raw_checkpoint()
data.tl.normalize_total(); data.tl.log1p()
data.tl.highly_variable_genes(); data.tl.pca(); data.tl.neighbors(); data.tl.leiden()
tools.runtime: Minutes to hours; Stereo-seq FOVs are huge (cm-scale), memory-bound.
tools.limitations: Bin-based analysis is not single-cell. Cell segmentation from ssDNA is imperfect. API differs from scanpy; conversion to AnnData needed for many downstream tools.

tools.name: Cellpose
tools.why: General-purpose deep-learning cell/nucleus segmentation from images (DAPI, membrane, H&E). The most widely used image-based segmenter; strong pretrained models plus fine-tuning.
tools.code:
from cellpose import models
model = models.Cellpose(gpu=True, model_type='nuclei')
masks, flows, styles, diams = model.eval(image, diameter=None, channels=[0,0])
tools.runtime: Seconds per FOV on GPU; minutes-to-hours for a whole large section. CPU is far slower.
tools.limitations: Image-based, so it segments morphology, not transcripts - dense/overlapping cells and weak membrane staining cause over/under-segmentation. Diameter must be roughly right. Does NOT solve segmentation; always inspect masks.

tools.name: StarDist
tools.why: Star-convex polygon nucleus segmentation; excellent on DAPI nuclei and the default nucleus caller inside bin2cell for Visium HD.
tools.code:
from stardist.models import StarDist2D
model = StarDist2D.from_pretrained('2D_versatile_fluo')
labels, _ = model.predict_instances(normalize(dapi_image))
tools.runtime: Seconds per tile on GPU.
tools.limitations: Nucleus-only (no cytoplasm), so it under-counts transcripts in the cytoplasm unless you expand nuclei. Struggles with non-convex or clumped nuclei.

tools.name: Baysor
tools.install: Download binary from GitHub releases (Julia); or run via sopa. No pip.
tools.why: Transcript-based segmentation: uses the spatial density of transcripts themselves (optionally with a nuclei prior) rather than only a stain. Frequently improves imaging-platform boundaries over vendor defaults, especially where membranes aren't stained.
tools.code:
# Command line (Julia binary):
# baysor run -s 50 -x x -y y -g gene transcripts.csv -p --prior-segmentation-confidence 0.5
# Or orchestrated: sopa segmentation baysor experiment.zarr --config config.toml
tools.runtime: Minutes to hours; scales with transcript count. Parallelizable.
tools.limitations: Sensitive to the scale parameter (approx cell radius). Can merge/split cells in dense regions. Julia install friction; most users drive it via sopa. Not a solved solution - validate against morphology.

tools.name: ProSeg
tools.install: cargo install proseg  (or download release binary; also available via sopa)
tools.why: Fast probabilistic transcript-based segmentation designed for large imaging datasets; models transcripts as a spatial point process and is markedly faster than Baysor at similar quality.
tools.code:
# proseg --xenium transcripts.csv.gz --nthreads 8 -o output/
# Outputs cell polygons + cell-by-gene matrix
tools.runtime: Minutes for datasets that take Baysor hours; designed for speed.
tools.limitations: Newer and less battle-tested than Baysor. Like all segmenters, dense tissue and 3D overlap still cause errors; inspect results.

tools.name: bin2cell
tools.why: Purpose-built for Visium HD: uses the H&E/DAPI image (via StarDist) plus 2um bin expression to reconstruct cell-like objects from 2um bins. The current practical answer for 'cells' from Visium HD.
tools.code:
import bin2cell as b2c
adata = b2c.read_visium('binned_outputs/square_002um/', source_image_path='he.tif')
b2c.scaled_he_image(adata)
b2c.stardist(...)  # nucleus labels
cdata = b2c.bin_to_cell(adata, ...)
tools.runtime: Minutes to hours depending on section size and StarDist backend.
tools.limitations: Bin-to-cell is inherently approximate; boundaries come from nuclei expansion, not true membranes. Sparse 2um bins mean noisy per-cell counts. Active research area.

tools.name: DeepCell / Mesmer
tools.why: Mesmer is a whole-cell segmentation model trained on tissue (nuclear + membrane channels); strong when you have a good membrane/cytoplasm marker.
tools.code:
from deepcell.applications import Mesmer
app = Mesmer()
# im shape (1, H, W, 2): channel 0 nuclear, channel 1 membrane
masks = app.predict(im, image_mpp=0.5)
tools.runtime: Seconds per FOV on GPU.
tools.limitations: Needs a real membrane channel to shine; nuclear-only inputs give nuclear-like masks. TensorFlow dependency can be heavy to install.

tools.name: Harmony (harmonypy)
tools.why: Fast, embedding-level batch correction integrated into scanpy (sc.external.pp.harmony_integrate). A sensible default first attempt because it's fast, corrects the PCA embedding (not counts), and is easy to compare against no-correction.
tools.code:
import scanpy as sc
sc.pp.pca(adata)
sc.external.pp.harmony_integrate(adata, key='batch')
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, use_rep='X_pca_harmony'); sc.tl.leiden(adata)
tools.runtime: Seconds to minutes for hundreds of thousands of cells.
tools.limitations: Corrects an embedding, not expression - you cannot get 'corrected counts' for DE. Can over-integrate and merge genuinely distinct populations; ALWAYS verify known markers/conditions survive. Batch correction is not solved.

tools.name: scvi-tools (scVI / scANVI)
tools.why: Deep generative integration (scVI) and semi-supervised label transfer (scANVI); also hosts DestVI (spatial deconvolution) and Stereoscope. Preferred when you need a probabilistic model, count-level batch correction, or reference label transfer in one framework.
tools.code:
import scvi
scvi.model.SCVI.setup_anndata(adata, batch_key='batch')
model = scvi.model.SCVI(adata); model.train()
adata.obsm['X_scVI'] = model.get_latent_representation()
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, use_rep='X_scVI')
tools.runtime: Minutes to hours; GPU strongly recommended. Training time scales with cells and epochs.
tools.limitations: Needs enough cells per batch to train well; stochastic (set seeds). Can still over-correct. GPU effectively required for large data. Not solved - validate integration.

tools.name: Scanorama
tools.why: Panorama-stitching integration that also returns batch-corrected expression (not just an embedding), useful when a downstream tool needs corrected features. Good second method to cross-check Harmony/scVI.
tools.code:
import scanorama
corrected = scanorama.correct_scanpy(list_of_adatas, return_dimred=True)
tools.runtime: Minutes; memory grows with number of datasets.
tools.limitations: Assumes shared cell types across batches; can distort when compositions differ strongly. Corrected expression should not be over-trusted for DE.

tools.name: Seurat (RPCA / CCA integration)
tools.why: The R-ecosystem standard: SCTransform normalization + anchor-based (RPCA/CCA) integration + Azimuth reference mapping. Choose if your lab lives in R.
tools.code:
# R
obj.list <- SplitObject(obj, split.by='batch')
obj.list <- lapply(obj.list, SCTransform)
anchors <- FindIntegrationAnchors(obj.list, reduction='rpca')
integrated <- IntegrateData(anchors)
tools.runtime: Minutes to hours; RPCA faster than CCA on large data.
tools.limitations: Memory-heavy in R for large data. Same over/under-correction risks as all integration. Crossing between R and Python ecosystems adds friction.

tools.name: PASTE / PASTE2
tools.install: pip install paste-bio   # PASTE; PASTE2 from the raphael-group repo
tools.why: Optimal-transport alignment of serial sections using both spatial coordinates and expression. PASTE builds a consensus/stacked 3D reconstruction; PASTE2 handles partial overlap between adjacent sections (the common real case). The standard OT baseline for serial-section registration.
tools.code:
import paste as pst
# pairwise alignment of adjacent slices
pi = pst.pairwise_align(sliceA, sliceB)
# or full stack -> common coordinates
center_slice, pis = pst.center_align(reference, [s1, s2, s3])
tools.runtime: Seconds to minutes per section pair; OT scales with spot count (subsample very large sections).
tools.limitations: Assumes adjacent sections are similar; large biological change or big z-gaps break it. Partial-overlap fraction (PASTE2 s) must be set. Alignment can look numerically fine while anatomy is subtly wrong - inspect visually.

tools.name: Sutura Align (this project)
tools.why: Our in-house serial-section alignment. HONEST SCOPE: it does two things. (1) It routes a section pair to the best-performing existing aligner for that data regime (PASTE2 is the usual winner), rather than assuming one method always wins. (2) When a fit-residual gate indicates the base alignment is trustworthy, it applies an optional per-pair gated refinement that measurably improves on PASTE2 in our internal benchmarks (e.g. lower alignment error on held-out DLPFC/breast pairs). It does NOT invent a new registration paradigm and does NOT solve distortion/tears.
tools.code:
from workflow_recommend import sutura_align_note
# Prototype note only. In production this wraps PASTE2 + a gated refinement step:
#   1. align with PASTE2
#   2. compute fit residual; if below gate threshold, apply piecewise refinement
#   3. else fall back to the raw PASTE2 mapping (do no harm)
tools.runtime: PASTE2 base cost plus a small refinement overhead (seconds per pair).
tools.limitations: Research-stage. The refinement only helps when the gate fires; when it doesn't, you get PASTE2 unchanged (by design, to avoid making things worse). Cross-donor synthetic residuals do not transfer; refinement is learned per pair. Not a substitute for visual QC of anatomy.

tools.name: STalign
tools.why: Diffeomorphic (LDDMM) alignment that models smooth nonlinear tissue deformation - better than affine/OT when sections are warped or distorted. Works from images or cell centroids, good for imaging platforms.
tools.code:
from STalign import STalign
# build velocity field mapping source -> target
params = {'niter': 2000, 'epV': 10}
out = STalign.LDDMM([Y,X], I, [Y2,X2], J, **params)
tools.runtime: Minutes per pair on GPU; slower on CPU.
tools.limitations: Nonlinear registration can over-warp and hallucinate correspondence if under-constrained. Needs sensible initialization. Diffeomorphic != correct; validate landmarks.

tools.name: GPSA
tools.why: Gaussian-Process Spatial Alignment learns a common coordinate system across slices probabilistically, giving uncertainty on the mapping. Useful when you want a principled shared 3D frame with uncertainty rather than a point estimate.
tools.code:
from gpsa import VariationalGPSA
model = VariationalGPSA(...)
# fit shared coordinate system across multiple slices
tools.runtime: Minutes to hours; GP inference is compute-heavy and scales poorly with spot count (subsample).
tools.limitations: Scales poorly to many spots; often needs subsampling. Research-stage with real setup friction. In our internal tests it did not close the cross-donor gap.

tools.name: moscot
tools.why: Scalable optimal-transport toolkit (from the scverse/Theis lab) covering spatial mapping and serial-section alignment with GPU-backed solvers that scale better than classic PASTE on large data. Also does mapping single cells to space.
tools.code:
from moscot.problems.space import AlignmentProblem
ap = AlignmentProblem(adata).prepare(batch_key='slice').solve()
ap.align(reference='0')
tools.runtime: Seconds to minutes on GPU even for large sections; better scaling than vanilla OT.
tools.limitations: Younger API. OT-based, so shares OT assumptions (similar adjacent sections). Verify alignment visually.

tools.name: Tangram
tools.why: Maps a single-cell reference onto spatial data by learning a cell-to-spot probability matrix; used for label transfer (imaging) and deconvolution (spots), and to impute genes outside a targeted panel.
tools.code:
import tangram as tg
tg.pp_adatas(adata_sc, adata_sp, genes=markers)
tg.map_cells_to_space(adata_sc, adata_sp, device='cuda')
tg.project_cell_annotations(adata_map, adata_sp, annotation='cell_type')
tools.runtime: Minutes on GPU; scales with cells x spots.
tools.limitations: Requires a matched single-cell reference; quality is capped by that reference. Mapping is soft - hard labels can be misleading. GPU recommended.

tools.name: CellTypist
tools.why: Fast logistic-regression cell-type classifier with many prebuilt immune/tissue models; great first-pass automated annotation for single-cell-resolution spatial data. You can also train on your own reference.
tools.code:
import celltypist
pred = celltypist.annotate(adata, model='Immune_All_Low.pkl', majority_voting=True)
adata = pred.to_adata()
tools.runtime: Seconds to minutes.
tools.limitations: Prebuilt models are trained on scRNA and may not match a targeted spatial panel or your tissue/disease state. Confident labels can be wrong for novel states - confirm with markers.

tools.name: Azimuth (Seurat reference mapping)
tools.why: Supervised reference mapping onto curated HuBMAP/atlas references with hierarchical labels and per-cell mapping scores. Strong when a well-matched Azimuth reference exists for your organ.
tools.code:
# R
library(Azimuth)
obj <- RunAzimuth(obj, reference='kidneyref')
tools.runtime: Minutes.
tools.limitations: Only as good as the available reference; no reference for your organ/condition means no good answer. R ecosystem. Mapping scores must be checked to catch out-of-reference cells.

tools.name: popV
tools.why: Runs many annotation methods (scANVI, kNN, Random Forest, Celltypist, ...) against a reference and reports consensus + agreement, so you can see where annotations are uncertain rather than trusting one classifier.
tools.code:
from popv.preprocessing import Process_Query
# builds a query object, runs an ensemble of annotation algorithms, outputs consensus
tools.runtime: Minutes to tens of minutes (runs several methods).
tools.limitations: Heavier setup; consensus of biased methods can still be jointly wrong. Needs a good reference.

tools.name: cell2location
tools.why: Bayesian spot deconvolution that estimates absolute cell-type abundance per spot from a matched single-cell reference. Well-validated on Visium; models technical variation explicitly. A default choice for Visium deconvolution.
tools.code:
import cell2location as c2l
# 1) estimate reference signatures from scRNA
# 2) map to spatial:
mod = c2l.models.Cell2location(adata_vis, cell_state_df=ref_sig, N_cells_per_location=8)
mod.train(max_epochs=30000)
adata_vis = mod.export_posterior(adata_vis)
tools.runtime: Tens of minutes to a few hours on GPU (long training); GPU strongly recommended.
tools.limitations: Requires a matched scRNA reference; missing cell types produce wrong abundances. Long training. N_cells_per_location prior matters. Validate against known anatomy.

tools.name: RCTD (spacexr)
tools.why: Robust Cell Type Decomposition; fast, well-validated, and handles platform effects between reference and spatial. 'doublet mode' is popular for near-single-cell spots. The R-side default for deconvolution.
tools.code:
# R
reference <- Reference(sc_counts, cell_types)
puck <- SpatialRNA(coords, counts)
rctd <- create.RCTD(puck, reference); rctd <- run.RCTD(rctd, doublet_mode='doublet')
tools.runtime: Minutes to tens of minutes; faster than cell2location.
tools.limitations: Reference-dependent like all deconvolution. R ecosystem. Doublet mode assumes few cells per spot - wrong for large multi-cell spots.

tools.name: DestVI (scvi-tools)
tools.why: Deep-learning deconvolution that also estimates continuous within-cell-type variation per spot, inside the scvi-tools framework - convenient if you already use scVI/scANVI.
tools.code:
from scvi.model import CondSCVI, DestVI
sc_model = CondSCVI(sc_adata); sc_model.train()
st_model = DestVI.from_rna_model(st_adata, sc_model); st_model.train()
st_adata.obsm['proportions'] = st_model.get_proportions()
tools.runtime: Tens of minutes on GPU (trains two models).
tools.limitations: Two-stage training, GPU recommended; reference-dependent. Continuous sub-states can overfit with small references.

tools.name: SPOTlight
tools.why: NMF-based deconvolution, lightweight and fast; a reasonable R alternative or cross-check to RCTD/cell2location.
tools.code:
# R
res <- SPOTlight(x=sc_counts, y=spatial_counts, groups=cell_types, mgs=marker_genes)
tools.runtime: Minutes.
tools.limitations: Generally less accurate than cell2location/RCTD in benchmarks; reference-dependent. R ecosystem.

tools.name: SpaGCN
tools.why: Graph convolutional network that integrates expression, spatial location, and (optionally) histology into spatial domains. Widely cited, works across platforms, relatively light.
tools.code:
import SpaGCN as spg
adj = spg.calculate_adj_matrix(x=x, y=y, histology=False)
clf = spg.SpaGCN(); clf.set_l(l)
clf.train(adata, adj, num_pcs=50, n_clusters=7)
domains = clf.predict()
tools.runtime: Minutes; GPU optional.
tools.limitations: Number of domains is user-specified. Histology integration needs a registered image. Sensitive to the smoothing parameter l.

tools.name: BayesSpace
tools.why: Bayesian spatial clustering with a neighbor-smoothing prior; also does sub-spot resolution enhancement for Visium. A well-validated domain caller for spot data.
tools.code:
# R
sce <- spatialPreprocess(sce, platform='Visium')
sce <- qTune(sce, qs=seq(2,10))
sce <- spatialCluster(sce, q=7)
tools.runtime: Minutes to tens of minutes (MCMC).
tools.limitations: Designed for lattice (Visium) geometry; less natural for irregular imaging coordinates. Number of clusters q must be chosen. R ecosystem.

tools.name: STAGATE
tools.why: Graph attention autoencoder that learns a spatially-aware embedding; often gives cleaner domains than plain Leiden and scales to imaging data. Popular in recent benchmarks.
tools.code:
import STAGATE_pyG as STAGATE
adata = STAGATE.Cal_Spatial_Net(adata, rad_cutoff=150)
adata = STAGATE.train_STAGATE(adata)
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, use_rep='STAGATE'); sc.tl.leiden(adata)
tools.runtime: Minutes on GPU.
tools.limitations: Radius/neighbor cutoff must suit the platform scale. GPU recommended for large data. Embedding quality varies with tissue.

tools.name: GraphST
tools.why: Graph contrastive self-supervised model for spatial clustering that can also horizontally integrate multiple sections into shared domains - handy when you want domains AND cross-section integration together.
tools.code:
from GraphST import GraphST
model = GraphST.GraphST(adata, device=device)
adata = model.train()
# then clustering on adata.obsm['emb']
tools.runtime: Minutes on GPU.
tools.limitations: Younger tool; results sensitive to graph construction. Its integration shares the general over-correction risk.

tools.name: BANKSY
tools.why: Augments each cell's expression with its neighborhood mean and azimuthal gradient, then clusters. One knob (lambda) smoothly trades off cell typing vs domain segmentation; very fast and scales to millions of cells. Increasingly a default for large imaging data.
tools.code:
# Concept: build BANKSY matrix (own + neighbour features), then standard clustering
# lambda ~0.2 for cell typing, ~0.8 for spatial domains
from banksy_py import ...  # see repo; integrates with AnnData/scanpy
tools.runtime: Seconds to minutes; scales well to very large datasets.
tools.limitations: lambda is a user choice that changes results meaningfully. Neighborhood features can blur sharp boundaries. Still emerging API.

tools.name: SpatialDE
tools.why: Gaussian-process test for spatially variable genes; classic, easy to run for a first SVG list.
tools.code:
import SpatialDE
results = SpatialDE.run(coords, expression_df)  # expression_df: spots x genes
tools.runtime: Minutes; the original is slow on large data (see SPARK-X / squidpy for speed).
tools.limitations: Slow at scale; superseded on speed by SPARK-X. SVG != biologically meaningful; interpret with anatomy. Confounded by composition.

tools.name: SPARK / SPARK-X
tools.why: SPARK-X is a fast, scalable non-parametric test for spatially variable genes designed for large datasets (hundreds of thousands of cells). The go-to when SpatialDE is too slow.
tools.code:
# R
sparkx_res <- sparkx(count_matrix, location_matrix, numCores=8)
tools.runtime: Minutes even for large data (SPARK-X); SPARK (the parametric version) is slower.
tools.limitations: R ecosystem. Reports spatial variability, not causal/biological meaning. Composition confounding remains.

tools.name: Hotspot
tools.why: Finds genes with spatial (or lineage) autocorrelation and groups them into co-varying modules - useful when you want spatial gene programs, not just a flat SVG list.
tools.code:
import hotspot
hs = hotspot.Hotspot(adata, model='danb', latent_obsm_key='spatial')
hs.create_knn_graph(n_neighbors=30)
hs_results = hs.compute_autocorrelations()
modules = hs.create_modules()
tools.runtime: Minutes.
tools.limitations: Module count/thresholds are choices. Interpretation still needs biology.

tools.name: PyDESeq2 (pseudobulk DE)
tools.why: For disease-vs-control (or any condition) comparisons, the statistically correct approach is PSEUDOBULK: sum counts per sample x cell-type, then run DESeq2-style negative-binomial DE across samples. PyDESeq2 does this in Python; decoupler builds the pseudobulk matrix. This avoids the pseudo-replication that inflates per-cell DE false positives.
tools.code:
import decoupler as dc
from pydeseq2.dds import DeseqDataSet
from pydeseq2.ds import DeseqStats
pdata = dc.get_pseudobulk(adata, sample_col='sample', groups_col='cell_type')
dds = DeseqDataSet(adata=pdata, design_factors='condition'); dds.deseq2()
stat = DeseqStats(dds, contrast=['condition','disease','control']); stat.summary()
tools.runtime: Seconds to minutes (operates on the small pseudobulk matrix).
tools.limitations: Needs biological replicates (multiple samples per condition) - with n=1 per group there is no valid statistic. Cell-type assignment errors propagate. Not spatial per se; pair with spatial context.

tools.name: LIANA+
tools.why: Consensus ligand-receptor inference that aggregates many methods/databases and integrates with spatial and multi-omics workflows; better than trusting a single LR method/database.
tools.code:
import liana as li
li.mt.rank_aggregate(adata, groupby='cell_type', use_raw=False)
li.pl.dotplot(adata, ...)
tools.runtime: Minutes.
tools.limitations: LR inference is correlational and database-dependent; co-expression is not signaling. Spatial context should be added (proximity), not assumed.

tools.name: CellPhoneDB
tools.why: Curated ligand-receptor database with permutation testing for enriched interactions between cell types; very widely used and cited, with a well-maintained complex-aware database.
tools.code:
from cellphonedb.src.core.methods import cpdb_statistical_analysis_method
cpdb_statistical_analysis_method.call(meta_file_path=meta, counts_file_path=counts, ...)
tools.runtime: Minutes to tens of minutes (permutations).
tools.limitations: Not inherently spatial (add proximity separately). Permutation p-values depend on grouping. Database is human-centric.

tools.name: COMMOT
tools.why: Spatially-informed cell-cell communication via collective optimal transport that respects physical distance and ligand diffusion range - a genuinely spatial LR method rather than a non-spatial one applied post-hoc.
tools.code:
import commot as ct
ct.tl.spatial_communication(adata, database_name='cellchat', df_ligrec=lr, dis_thr=200)
tools.runtime: Minutes; OT scales with cell count.
tools.limitations: Still requires an LR database; diffusion range is an assumption. Emerging tool. Outputs are hypotheses.

tools.name: napari (+ napari-spatialdata)
tools.why: Interactive n-dimensional image viewer; the practical tool for inspecting segmentation masks and for viewing 3D reconstructed serial-section stacks. napari-spatialdata links it to SpatialData objects.
tools.code:
import napari
from napari_spatialdata import Interactive
Interactive(sdata)  # explore images, shapes, points, tables interactively
tools.runtime: Interactive; large images need lazy/Dask loading.
tools.limitations: Desktop GUI (awkward on headless servers). Large datasets need downsampling/lazy loading. Not for automated reporting.

tools.name: Vitessce
tools.why: Web-based, shareable interactive visualization of multi-modal spatial data (images + cells + expression), embeddable in notebooks and served to collaborators without local installs.
tools.code:
from vitessce import VitessceConfig
vc = VitessceConfig.from_object(adata, schema_version='1.0.16')
vc.widget()
tools.runtime: Interactive; needs data converted to Zarr/OME.
tools.limitations: Setup/data-conversion overhead. Best for sharing, less for deep single-user exploration than napari.

tools.name: TissUUmaps
tools.why: Lightweight browser-based viewer built for millions of transcript points overlaid on whole-slide images - good for imaging platforms where you want to eyeball transcripts vs tissue.
tools.code: # tissuumaps  # launches the viewer; load image + marker (transcript) CSVs
tools.runtime: Interactive.
tools.limitations: Viewer only (no analysis). Best for QC/exploration of imaging data.
